processing: Ripe pu-erh combined with jasmine. In classic jasmine scenting, tea rests with fresh blossoms and absorbs their aroma over repeated rounds; at least one maker of this tea instead presses dried jasmine flowers in with the leaf, and methods vary.
harvest_season: No defined tea season. Jasmine itself is a summer flower, and the base is ordinary ripe pu-erh of varying age.
appearance_dry: Dark brown ripe leaf, often in small tuos or pressed pieces, sometimes with pale flower remains.
appearance_liquor: Dark reddish-brown and clear, as is typical of ripe pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Soft dark leaf, with any flower remains pale against it.
taste_profile: Typically the earthy, smooth base of ripe pu-erh with a sweet jasmine perfume on top, strongest in the first steeps.

brewing.notes: Rinse quickly, since the rinse carries aroma away. Keep steeps short and use a pot you do not mind dedicating to scented tea.

vintage_note: Sold as a ready-to-drink tea, usually with little emphasis on year. Scent fades with time, so it is best drunk within a few years, unlike unscented ripe pu-erh, where age is part of the appeal. Store it apart from other tea.
description:
This is ripe pu-erh with jasmine aroma added, sold in forms such as small tuos. Two familiar Chinese tea ideas meet here: the dark, smooth base of shu and the perfume of jasmine scenting.

The method behind jasmine tea is a slow exchange: leaf and blossom sit together, the flowers give off scent and the tea takes it up. Not every jasmine shu is made this way: one seller describes dried jasmine flowers pressed in with the leaf, so ask what you are buying.

Expect the scent first and the earth underneath. The pairing softens the pile note of a plain shu. Short steeps keep the two in balance, and the jasmine fades after a few rounds.

Ask how it was scented and look for a natural floral smell rather than a sharp, soapy one. Treat it as an everyday tea and do not pay a premium for age.
history: Little is documented about when jasmine-scented ripe pu-erh first appeared. Jasmine scenting has its own long history in Chinese tea, mostly on green bases, while this version is a commercial variation made by various producers, with no known originator.
